body_html:
Spanish terms of endearment are everywhere: between couples, from parents to children, between friends and even from a shopkeeper to a regular customer. Some translate neatly (mi amor, “my love”); others sound strange in English (gordo, literally “fat”), yet are deeply affectionate in context. As a translator I find these words some of the hardest to render, because their warmth lives in tone, region and relationship. Here are 30 of the most common, with notes on who says them.

Key takeaways
  • Mi amor, cariño and cielo are safe and understood everywhere.
  • Diminutives (-ito, -ita) make words softer: amorcito, gordita.
  • Some nicknames sound rude when translated literally but are loving in context.
  • Many terms are used for children and partners alike; tone tells the difference.
{{toc}}

Classic Spanish terms of endearment

SpanishLiteral meaningUsed with
mi amormy lovePartners, children; very common
cariñoaffection, darlingPartners, children, friends (Spain especially)
cielo / mi cielosky, heavenPartners, children
mi vidamy lifePartners, children
corazónheartPartners, children, sometimes strangers kindly
tesorotreasureChildren, partners
mi rey / mi reinamy king / my queenPartners, children (common in Latin America)
mi media naranjamy half orangeYour soulmate, “other half”
bebé / bebitobabyPartners
mi príncipe / mi princesamy prince / princessChildren, playful with partners

Nicknames that sound strange in English

These are the ones that surprise learners. Literally they describe appearance, but in many families they are pure affection.

  • gordo / gorda, gordito / gordita: literally “fat”. Common between partners and family in much of Latin America, with no reference to weight.
  • flaco / flaca: literally “skinny”. Common in Argentina, Uruguay and Peru for a partner or friend.
  • negro / negra, negrito / negrita: used affectionately in parts of Latin America, regardless of skin color. Outside that cultural context, avoid it.
  • viejo / vieja: literally “old”. Used by some couples for each other, and by young people for their parents.
  • chino / china: “curly-haired” in Mexico; also used affectionately in parts of South America.

The lesson: never translate these word for word, and don’t use them yourself until you have heard them used warmly by people around you.

{{image:2}}

Diminutives: the secret ingredient

Adding -ito or -ita to almost any word makes it smaller, softer and more affectionate: amor → amorcito, corazón → corazoncito, mamá → mamita, abuela → abuelita. In some regions people use -ico / -ica (Costa Rica, parts of Colombia) or -ín / -ina (northern Spain). The Real Academia Española describes these suffixes as expressing smallness and affection, and in everyday speech the affection is often the main point.

{{book:love-slowly}}

Terms of endearment for children

  • mi niño / mi niña: my boy / my girl (also used for adults you love)
  • chiquito / chiquita: little one
  • mijo / mija: from mi hijo / mi hija; used by parents and grandparents, and even for non-relatives in Mexico and the US Southwest
  • nene / nena: baby, kid (also for partners in some places)
  • peque: short for pequeño, little one (Spain)

Playful nicknames between couples

  • osito / osita: little bear, like “teddy bear”
  • gordi: a cute, shortened gordo / gorda
  • churri: sweetie (Spain, informal)
  • bombón: chocolate treat, “hottie”
  • mi cielito: my little heaven
  • papi / mami: used between couples in parts of Latin America; can sound forward or sexual from someone you don’t know
{{image:3}}

How to use them naturally

Put the nickname at the start or end of a sentence: Buenos días, cariño, ¿Qué tal tu día, mi amor?, Te extraño, gordi. In texts, they pair beautifully with the phrases in {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}. And if you are not sure whether to say te quiero or te amo along with them, read {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}.

Terms of endearment by region

RegionNicknames you’ll hear often
Spaincariño, cielo, churri, peque, guapa/guapo (even between friends)
Mexicomi amor, mi vida, gordo/gorda, mijo/mija, chula
Argentina and Uruguaymi amor, flaco/flaca, gordi, bebé
Colombiami amor, mi vida, mi rey/mi reina, bebé
Caribbeanmi amor, mi cielo, papi/mami (between couples), mi negra/mi negro

These are tendencies, not rules. Families and friend groups develop their own vocabulary, which is part of the charm.

What to call your partner’s family

If you are dating someone from a Spanish-speaking family, you will hear these words too: suegro and suegra (father- and mother-in-law), cuñado and cuñada (brother- and sister-in-law) and, for the parents of your child’s spouse, consuegros. Many families also use loving nicknames for in-laws, such as suegrita. You’ll find more in {{link:meeting-your-partners-family-in-spanish|meeting your partner’s family in Spanish}}.

Common mistakes

  • Using mami or papi with someone you just met. It can sound vulgar.
  • Translating gordita as an insult. In context it is usually tender.
  • Copying a nickname from a song. Lyrics exaggerate. Start with mi amor or cariño.
  • Getting the gender wrong. mi rey for a man, mi reina for a woman; cariño and cielo work for anyone.

Terms of endearment are part of everyday affection in Spanish. For more real-life situations, from dates to family dinners, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

To use these names in a message, see {{list:birthday-wishes-for-boyfriend-in-spanish|birthday wishes for a boyfriend;spanish-quotes-about-love|Spanish quotes about love}}.

{{/if}}

Final thoughts

The sweetest Spanish nickname is the one your loved ones already use. Listen first, start with the safe classics and let the more colorful ones come naturally. A simple mi amor said warmly beats any rare word.

faq.q: What is the most common Spanish term of endearment?
faq.a: Mi amor (my love) is probably the most common, along with cariño and cielo. All three are understood and used across the Spanish-speaking world.

faq.q: Is gordo an insult in Spanish?
faq.a: Literally it means “fat”, but between partners and family in much of Latin America gordo or gordita is an affectionate nickname with no reference to weight.
Mija comes from mi hija, “my daughter”. Parents and grandparents use it affectionately, and in Mexico and the US Southwest it is often used for any young woman.
